function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your own CI/CD pipeline).  
I’ll also show you the exact contents of the files that should be generated so you can verify them before committing.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re working on a fork, replace `git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` with the SSH URL of your fork.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repository

Run the helper function (if you have it available) or simply inspect the tree:

```bash
tree -a
```

If you have the `analyse_repo_contents` tool exposed, you could call it like this:

```json
{
  "directory_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "include_subdirectories": true,
  "excluded_files": ["README.md", ".gitignore"],
  "language_threshold": 10.0
}
```

The expected output will tell you that **JavaScript/Node.js** dominates the repo (≈ 90 % of the source files).

---

## 3️⃣ Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# 3.1 Dockerfile – Node.js + Alpine
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Build the app (if you have a build step)
RUN npm run build || true

# Final stage – minimal runtime image
FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the built artifacts & node_modules from builder
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist   # adjust if you don’t have a dist folder
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the official `node:18-alpine` image (small footprint).  
> * Multi‑stage build keeps the final image lean.  
> * Copies only what’s needed for production.  
> * Exposes port `3000` – change if your app uses a different port.

---

## 4️⃣ Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` (or split into separate `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`) with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 3 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app via a LoadBalancer (cloud provider will provision an external IP).  
> * Maps external port `80` → internal port `3000`.

---

## 5️⃣ Add a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: k8s-deployment.yaml
        images: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub (you’ll need to store credentials in repo secrets).  
> * Optionally deploys to a Kubernetes cluster if you have a `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` secret.

---

## 6️⃣ Stage, commit, and push

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **After pushing**  
> * The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run.  
> * Once the image is pushed, the optional deployment step will apply the new image to your cluster.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .

# Run the container locally
docker run -p 3000:3000 test-nodejs-welcome
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is reachable.

---

That’s it! You now have a fully automated pipeline that builds a Docker image on every push to `main`, pushes it to Docker Hub, and optionally deploys it to Kubernetes. Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or service type to suit your environment.
